problem: Given the function $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{{e}^{x}},$ which of the following statements are true?
worked_solution:
First, we find the stationary points. Differentiating $f(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{2x{e}^{x}-({x}^{2}+1){e}^{x}}{{e}^{2x}} \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{2}-2x+1}{{e}^{x}} \\  & =-\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{{e}^{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ gives

$$
-\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{{e}^{x}}\,⟹\,x=1.
$$

Note that we used the fact that ${e}^{x}>0$ for all values of $x.$

So, $x=1$ is the only stationary point of $f(x).$ Next, to determine whether this point is a local maximum or minimum, we use the first derivative test.

Let's choose the test points $x=0,2$ and evaluate the first derivative at these points.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(0) & =-\frac{(0-1)^{2}}{{e}^{0}}=-1<0 \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =-\frac{(2-1)^{2}}{{e}^{2}}=-{e}^{-2}<0\end{aligned}
$$

We summarize the information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $0$ |  | $2$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $f$ | $↘$ |  | $↘$ |

The first derivative does not change sign at $x=1.$ Therefore, we conclude that $x=1$ is neither a minimum nor a maximum.

Therefore, the first derivative test shows that the function has no local extrema.

choices.value: There is a local maximum at $x=-1$
